\chapter{The Two Letters You Already Knew, and Six You Did Not}
\label{ch:ru-script-eight}
\hlchaptermodality{15}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write eight more Cyrillic letters from memory, sort each of them into true friend, false friend or new shape, and read an unstressed \ru{о} as an a -- which is the commonest thing an English reader gets wrong when reading Russian aloud.}

Eight letters sorted into two true friends, one false friend and five new shapes -- with the false friend named as the dangerous kind, because it is the only one that can be read confidently and wrongly.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[a]{\ru{а} — a true friend, and the sound Russian keeps landing on}

\label{lesson:RU-W07-a}



\begin{quote}
Write \ru{я}. A whole syllable in one letter, and nothing to do with the Latin R it resembles.

Three kinds of letter, you were told: \textbf{true friends}, \textbf{false friends}, and \textbf{new shapes}. This chapter opens with the two truest friends in the alphabet — and then shows you why they still catch people out.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\ru{а}
\end{quote}

A \textbf{true friend}, and about as true as they come. Same shape as Latin \emph{a}, and when it is stressed it says the \emph{a} of English \emph{father} — clean, open, and with none of the drift English \emph{a} has in \emph{cat}, \emph{cake} or \emph{call}.

Nothing to learn about the shape. What is worth learning is how \textbf{often} you will see it, and there is a reason for that beyond the alphabet, which the next letter explains.

Write it as you write a Latin \emph{a}. That is the whole instruction.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ru{а} — exactly the Latin letter
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{a} as in \emph{father}, held open, not the \emph{a} of \emph{cat}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which English \emph{a} is it — the one in \emph{cat}, or the one in \emph{father}? (\textbf{Father}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[o]{\ru{о} — the letter that is not always itself}

\label{lesson:RU-W07-o}



\begin{quote}
Write \ru{а}. Say it as in \emph{father}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\ru{о}
\end{quote}

Another \textbf{true friend} on the page: same shape as Latin \emph{o}, and when it is \textbf{stressed} it says the \emph{o} of English \emph{more}, shortened and rounded.

Write it as you write a Latin \emph{o}.

\begin{culture}
Now the part that matters, and it is worth more to you than the shape.

\textbf{When \ru{о} is NOT stressed, it is not pronounced o. It is pronounced a.}

Russian words carry exactly one stressed syllable, and every other vowel in the word relaxes towards the middle. For \ru{о}, that relaxation lands on \textbf{a}. So a word written with two \ru{о}'s, stressed on the second, comes out of a Russian mouth as \emph{a-o} — not \emph{o-o}.

This has a name — \textbf{akanye} — and you do not need the name. You need the habit:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{written \ru{о}, stressed} $\to$ say \textbf{o}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{written \ru{о}, unstressed} $\to$ say \textbf{a}
\end{quote}

One refinement, so the rule does not mislead you later: right \textbf{before} the stress the sound is a full \emph{a}. Further from the stress it relaxes further still, towards the \emph{uh} of English \emph{sofa}. Either way it is \textbf{not an o}, which is the part that matters.

It is the single commonest thing an English reader gets wrong when reading Russian aloud, because the letter is sitting right there on the page looking like an \emph{o} and behaving like an \emph{a}.

This is also why \textbf{\ru{а}} is the most-heard vowel in the language while not being the most-written one: it gets reinforcements from every unstressed \ru{о}.

\textbf{And this is why stress is marked in this book's romanizations rather than on the Cyrillic.} Russian text does not print stress marks — a native reader knows where the stress falls and needs no help. You do not know yet, so the romanization carries it, and the Cyrillic stays exactly as you would meet it in the world.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ru{о} — the Latin letter
  \item \emph{Say it:} a stressed \textbf{o}, then an unstressed one — and let the second become \textbf{a}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does the spelling change when the sound does? (\textbf{No} — the page keeps \ru{о}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[g]{\ru{г} — a corner, and a hard g}

\label{lesson:RU-W07-g}



\begin{quote}
Write \ru{о}. Then say what it becomes when it is not stressed.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\ru{г}
\end{quote}

A \textbf{new shape} — no Latin relative to mislead you. Two strokes meeting at a square corner: a horizontal across the top, and a vertical dropping from its left end. Like a Latin \textbf{F} with the middle bar removed, or a rotated \textbf{L}.

It says \textbf{g}, hard, as in English \emph{go} — \textbf{never} the soft \emph{g} of \emph{gem}. Russian spelling does not have that ambiguity, which is one fewer thing to carry than English asks of you.

It does have one twist, and you have already met it. In the ending \textbf{-\ru{ого}} (and \textbf{-\ru{его}}) this letter is written \ru{г} and \textbf{said \ru{в}} — which is why \emph{\ru{до} \ru{скорого}} comes out \emph{da-SKO-ra-va}. That ending is everywhere in Russian, so the exception is worth knowing on the day you learn the letter rather than being ambushed by it later. Everywhere else: hard g.

If it helps: this is the Greek \textbf{gamma}, squared off. Russian took its alphabet from Greek, and this is one of the letters where the descent is plain.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ru{г} — top horizontal, then the vertical down from its left end
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{g} as in \emph{go}, never as in \emph{gem}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Latin letter does it resemble with a bar removed? (\textbf{F}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kh]{\ru{х} — an x that is not an x}

\label{lesson:RU-W07-kh}



\begin{quote}
Write \ru{г}. A corner, and a hard g.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\ru{х}
\end{quote}

A \textbf{false friend}, and a well-disguised one. Two crossing diagonals — an exact Latin \textbf{x} on the page — and it does not say \emph{x}.

It says the sound at the end of Scottish \emph{loch} and German \emph{Bach}: a \textbf{breathy rasp} made at the back of the mouth, in the same place as \emph{k} but without ever closing it. Start to say \emph{k}, then leave the gap open and push air through.

Romanized in this book as \textbf{kh}, which is a warning label rather than a spelling: there is no \emph{k} and no \emph{h} in it, only the one rasping sound.

English has no letter for it, which is why English borrows it as \emph{ch} in \emph{loch} and \emph{Bach} and then most speakers say a \emph{k} anyway. You have the letter now, so you can do better than the borrowing.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ru{х} — two crossing diagonals, like a Latin x
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{kh} — start a \emph{k}, then leave it open and breathe through
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{loch}, the Scottish way, then just its ending
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is there a \emph{k} sound in it? (\textbf{No} — the mouth never closes.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[f]{\ru{ф} — a circle on a stick}

\label{lesson:RU-W07-f}



\begin{quote}
Write \ru{х}. Then make its sound without letting your mouth close.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\ru{ф}
\end{quote}

A \textbf{new shape}: a vertical stroke with a closed loop threaded onto it, the loop sitting on both sides of the line. Draw the vertical first, then the loop across it.

It says \textbf{f}, exactly as in English \emph{foot}. No trap at all.

This is Greek \textbf{phi}, and that ancestry shows in where you find it. Native Slavic words almost never contain \ru{ф} — nearly every Russian word with this letter came in from Greek or later from Western Europe. When you meet it, the word is very often one you can half-guess, because it was borrowed from a language you know.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ru{ф} — the vertical, then the loop threaded across it
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{f} as in \emph{foot}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Greek letter is it? (\textbf{Phi}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ts]{\ru{ц} — one letter for two sounds}

\label{lesson:RU-W07-ts}



\begin{quote}
Write \ru{ш} — three uprights standing on a base.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\ru{ц}
\end{quote}

A \textbf{new shape}, and one you should compare to \ru{ш} immediately, because they are close:

\begin{quote}
\ru{ш} — three uprights on a base, \textbf{nothing below the line}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ru{ц} — two uprights on a base, and a \textbf{small tail dropping below} at the right
\end{quote}

Two uprights instead of three, and a descender. That tail is doing real work: it is the only thing separating this letter from one you already know.

It says \textbf{ts}, the ending of English \emph{cats} — but as a \textbf{single} sound at the \textbf{start} of a word too, which English never asks of you. Say \emph{cats}, then say just its last two letters, then put a vowel after them.

One letter, one sound, even though English needs two letters to write it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ru{ф}, then \ru{ш}, then \ru{ц} — and check which one has the tail
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{cats}, then \textbf{ts} alone, then \textbf{tsa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does English write this sound with one letter or two? (\textbf{Two} — \emph{ts}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[y]{\ru{й} — \ru{и} in a hat}

\label{lesson:RU-W07-y-short}



\begin{quote}
Write \ru{ц}. Two uprights, base, tail.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\ru{й}
\end{quote}

\textbf{No new shape at all.} This is \textbf{\ru{и}}, which you have written since your very first letters, with a small curved cap sitting on top of it. The cap is called a \emph{breve}, and you draw the letter exactly as before and then add it last.

The cap changes the job. \textbf{\ru{и}} is a vowel, the \emph{ee} of \emph{see}. \textbf{\ru{й}} is a \textbf{consonant}: the \emph{y} of English \emph{boy} or \emph{yes}. Its formal name is \textquotedblleft{}short \ru{и}\textquotedblright{}, which describes it well — the same sound, clipped so short it stops being a syllable of its own and leans on the vowel beside it.

That is why it turns up glued to other vowels at the ends of words, and why it never carries the stress: it cannot, because it is not a syllable.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ru{и}, then add the cap to make \ru{й}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{ee}, then clip it to the \textbf{y} of \emph{boy}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Can this letter carry the stress of a word? (\textbf{No} — it is not a syllable.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yu]{\ru{ю} — a syllable in one letter, again}

\label{lesson:RU-W07-yu}



\begin{quote}
Write \ru{я}, then \ru{у}. One is a whole syllable; the other is the \emph{oo} that looks like a Latin y.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\ru{ю}
\end{quote}

A \textbf{new shape}, but a familiar idea. Two parts, joined: a \textbf{vertical stroke} on the left, and a \textbf{closed loop} to its right, tied to the vertical by a short horizontal at mid-height.

It says \textbf{yu} — the \emph{you} of English, or the \emph{u} of \emph{use}. One letter, two sounds, exactly the deal you already accepted with \textbf{\ru{я}} (\emph{ya}).

That is the pattern worth taking away: Russian has a small set of letters that each write a \textbf{y-glide plus a vowel} in a single shape. You have met two of them now. They are the reason a Russian word can look shorter than its pronunciation, and the reason counting letters is a poor guide to counting syllables.

Do not confuse its sound with \textbf{\ru{у}}, the \emph{oo} letter that looks like a Latin y. \ru{ю} is that sound with a \emph{y} welded to its front.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ru{ю} — the vertical, the loop, and the bar that ties them
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\ru{у}} (oo), then \textbf{\ru{ю}} (yoo) — the glide is the only difference
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\ru{я}}, then \textbf{\ru{ю}} — the same trick, two vowels
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ru{й}, then \ru{ю} — a capped letter, then a syllable-letter
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \ru{ю} the same sound as \ru{у}? (\textbf{No} — it is \ru{у} with a \emph{y} in front.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — eight more letters, sorted}

\label{lesson:RU-C15-practice}



\begin{quote}
Write \ru{а} and \ru{о}. Then say what happens to the second one when it is not the stressed vowel.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the three kinds, one more time}
You already have a way to sort any Cyrillic letter. Here are this chapter's eight, sorted:

\textbf{True friends} — the shape and the sound both match Latin:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{а}} \emph{a} · \textbf{\ru{о}} \emph{o}
\end{quote}

\textbf{False friend} — the Latin shape, a different sound:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{х}} \emph{kh}, the rasp in \emph{loch}
\end{quote}

\textbf{New shapes} — no Latin relative to help or mislead:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{г}} \emph{g} · \textbf{\ru{ф}} \emph{f} · \textbf{\ru{ц}} \emph{ts} · \textbf{\ru{ю}} \emph{yu}
\end{quote}

And one that fits none of the three, because it is not a new letter at all:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{й}} — \ru{и} wearing a cap
\end{quote}

Two, one, four and one. The single false friend is the one to drill, because a false friend is the only kind that can be read confidently and wrongly: a new shape stops you dead, but \ru{х} lets you read straight past it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Twenty-one letters before this chapter, and twenty-nine now. Russian has thirty-three.

Three of the eight cost you almost nothing. \textbf{\ru{а}} and \textbf{\ru{о}} were already yours from the Latin alphabet — the work in them was not the shape but \textbf{what unstressed \ru{о} does to your ear} — and \textbf{\ru{й}} is a letter you already write, wearing a cap.

That leaves \textbf{four genuinely new shapes} (\ru{г}, \ru{ф}, \ru{ц}, \ru{ю}) and \textbf{one false friend} (\ru{х}) to drill. Five letters of real work out of eight.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ru{а} \ru{о} \ru{г} \ru{х} \ru{ф} \ru{ц} \ru{й} \ru{ю} — all eight, in order, without looking above
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{kh}, the one that is not an x
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ru{ш}, then \ru{ц} — and check which one has the tail
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\ru{и}}, then \textbf{\ru{й}} — vowel, then consonant
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many of the thirty-three are now yours? (\textbf{Twenty-nine}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
